**Robert the Bruce and the Battle of Bannockburn**
Robert the Bruce was crowned King of Scots in 1306 and led the First War of Scottish Independence. At Bannockburn in 1314 he decisively defeated Edward II of England, killing the English knight Henry de Bohun in single combat at the start of the battle; his lieutenants included "Good Sir" James Douglas.

**William Wallace and the Battle of Stirling Bridge**
Wallace and Andrew Moray defeated an English army at Stirling Bridge in 1297, killing the English treasurer Hugh de Cressingham; Moray was mortally wounded there. Wallace was defeated by Edward I at Falkirk in 1298, where English longbowmen broke the Scots' schiltrons (dense rings of spearmen), and he was captured and executed in 1305. Blind Harry's poem The Wallace dramatized his career.

**Auld Alliance**
The long-standing alliance between Scotland and France against England, first concluded in 1295 when John Balliol's government allied with Philip IV ("the Fair") of France. It was renewed repeatedly until the Scottish Reformation in 1560.

**Acts of Union (1707) and the Darien Scheme**
The Acts of Union, passed under Queen Anne, merged the Kingdoms of Scotland and England into the Kingdom of Great Britain. Scotland's willingness was partly driven by the financial disaster of the Darien Scheme, a failed attempt in the late 1690s to found a Scottish colony on the Isthmus of Panama; in the Scottish Parliament, the independent Squadrone Volante joined the Court Party to pass the Union.

**Mary, Queen of Scots**
The daughter of James V, who became queen at six days old, was sent to France and married Francis II, and returned to Scotland as a Catholic ruler. Her secretary David Rizzio was murdered in a plot involving her husband Lord Darnley; after defeats at Carberry Hill and Langside she fled to England, where Elizabeth I imprisoned her and executed her in 1587 after Francis Walsingham uncovered the Babington Plot.

**Declaration of Arbroath**
A 1320 letter from Scottish barons to Pope John XXII asserting Scotland's independence and defending Robert the Bruce as king. Bruce had been excommunicated, and the letter asked the pope to recognize Scottish sovereignty against English claims.

**The "Great Cause" and Margaret, Maid of Norway**
After Alexander III died in 1286 when his horse went over the cliffs at Kinghorn, the Guardians of Scotland recognized his granddaughter Margaret, Maid of Norway, as queen. Her death in 1290 caused a succession dispute, the "Great Cause," which Edward I of England arbitrated in favor of John Balliol, setting the stage for the Wars of Independence.

**John Balliol, "Toom Tabard"**
The king chosen in the Great Cause, mocked as "Toom Tabard" ("empty coat") because he was seen as Edward I's puppet. After he defied Edward and allied with France, his army was routed at Dunbar in 1296 and he was forced to abdicate; his son Edward Balliol later led the "Disinherited" nobles against the Bruce dynasty.

**Murder of John Comyn**
In 1306 Robert the Bruce stabbed his rival John "the Red" Comyn to death before the altar of Greyfriars Church in Dumfries. The sacrilege got Bruce excommunicated; he then seized the crown but was soon defeated by the English at the Battle of Methven and forced into hiding.

**Edward I, "Hammer of the Scots"**
Edward I ("Longshanks") of England repeatedly invaded Scotland, removing the Stone of Scone and executing Wallace. During his 1304 siege of Stirling Castle he built the "Warwolf," the largest trebuchet ever made.

**Battle of Culloden and the Jacobite risings**
The Jacobites sought to restore the Catholic Stuarts (James II/VII and his heirs) to the throne. The 1745 rising of Bonnie Prince Charlie ended at Culloden Moor in 1746, where the Duke of Cumberland crushed the Highland army; afterward the Dress Act of 1746 banned tartan and Highland dress, and the power of the clan chiefs was broken.

**James VI and the Union of the Crowns**
The son of Mary, Queen of Scots, James VI inherited the English throne on Elizabeth I's death in 1603, becoming James I of England. This "Union of the Crowns" put both kingdoms under one monarch while they remained separate states until 1707; as English king he sponsored the King James Bible and survived the Gunpowder Plot.

**Covenanters, the Bishops' Wars, and John Knox**
John Knox led the Scottish Reformation and established Presbyterianism as Scotland's national church. When Charles I tried to impose an Anglican-style Book of Common Prayer in 1637, Scottish Covenanters revolted, fighting the Bishops' Wars of 1639–1640.

**Stone of Scone and Moot Hill**
The Stone of Scone (Stone of Destiny) was the stone on which Scottish kings were crowned at Scone, including on Moot Hill. Edward I carried it to Westminster Abbey in 1296; it was returned to Scotland in 1996.

**Highland Clearances**
The 18th- and 19th-century eviction of Highland tenant farmers (crofters) by landlords to make way for sheep farming, notoriously on the Sutherland estate, which Karl Marx condemned in Das Kapital. The Clearances, together with the collapse of the clan system after Culloden, emptied much of the Highlands.
